entries.title: Alabama
entries.answer: Follow Alabama from north to south and the land changes from ridges and valleys to a wide stretch of lower ground. Part of the Appalachian Mountains reaches into the northeast. Near the opposite end of the state, rivers empty into Mobile Bay, which opens toward the Gulf Coast. Montgomery, the state capital, sits inland on the Alabama River. That inland location is different from Mobile’s, where boats can travel between a bay and the open Gulf.
facts: Alabama joined the United States in 1819.

questions.text: How far south do the Appalachian Mountains reach?
What is the state just west of Alabama like?
How did people in Montgomery change who could sit where on a bus?

entries.title: Alaska
entries.answer: On a map, Alaska reaches far to the northwest of the other states. It shares a land border with Canada and has shores on both Arctic and Pacific waters. The Alaska Range has high peaks where snow can last through summer, while the southeast contains forested islands and long, narrow waterways. Juneau, the capital, is in that southeastern part. Alaska is the largest U.S. state by area, so the views and weather can change a lot across the state.
facts: Alaska became the 49th state in 1959.

questions.text: What country connects to Alaska by land?
How does a mountain glacier form and move?
What can grow where the ground stays cold?

entries.title: Altitude
entries.answer: Altitude describes how high something is compared with a chosen level. Maps often measure land height from sea level. Planes can also report how high they are above the ground directly below them, which is a different number. Higher in the air, there is less air pressing down, so the air is thinner. A breath at the top of a tall mountain contains less oxygen than a breath of the same size beside the sea.
facts: Two airplanes at the same height above sea level can be different heights above the ground below them.

questions.text: Which country shares the peak of Mount Everest with China?
Which African mountain rises high enough for snow or ice near the equator?
What gives you the pull you feel as weight?

entries.title: Amazon River
entries.answer: The Amazon begins with streams in the Andes and grows as more rivers join it on the way east. Rain falling across a wide part of South America feeds its huge river system. In wetter times of year, water can spread beyond the river’s banks into parts of the forest. Where the Amazon reaches the Atlantic, it sends enough fresh water into the ocean to affect conditions well beyond the river’s mouth.
facts: The Amazon carries more water to the ocean than any other river on Earth.

questions.text: Which mountains supply the Amazon with water near the start of its journey?
Which country contains the Amazon’s wide mouth?
How does water in rivers make its way back into the air?

entries.title: Andes Mountains
entries.answer: The Andes run like a high spine along the western side of South America. Far below the coast, a large piece of the ocean floor slides beneath the edge of the continent. That movement helps lift and squeeze rock, and it also helps feed eruptions in parts of the range. Hills, wide valleys, icy peaks, and even parts of great deserts belong to this long chain, so crossing it can take you through several climates.
facts: The Andes are the longest mountain range on land.
Many rivers that start in the Andes flow east toward the Atlantic.

questions.text: Which tall mountain range in Asia formed when two pieces of continent pushed into each other?
Where does some of the water from the eastern Andes flow?
What makes the rocky pieces of Earth’s outer shell move relative to each other?

entries.title: Antarctic Ice Sheet
entries.answer: Most of Antarctica is covered by a layer of ice thick enough to hide mountains and valleys beneath it. It formed as falling snow piled up over a very long time, squashing the air out of older layers and turning them into ice. The ice moves slowly toward the edges under its own weight. This sheet sits on land, while much of the ice around it floats on the ocean.
facts: In its thickest places the Antarctic Ice Sheet is more than four kilometers thick.
Most of the Antarctic continent could not be seen from the air without seeing through ice.

questions.text: Why do places near the poles have months when the Sun stays close to the horizon?
How does the world map divide land into continents including Antarctica?
Which northern island country also has large areas covered by moving ice?

entries.title: Are the Great Plains completely flat?
entries.answer: The Great Plains are a broad, open region east of the Rocky Mountains that runs through parts of the central United States and into Canada. In some places the horizon seems almost flat, but in others the land rolls, rises or breaks into river valleys. The land generally gets higher toward the Rockies. Grasses grew across large areas, and people now use parts of the plains for crops or grazing animals. Some stretches still have native grassland.
facts: The high plains near the mountains can be far above sea level even when they look flat.

questions.text: Where can tall prairie grass still grow in Kansas?
What landforms can you see on Nebraska’s plains?
How can steep ravines cut into an open plain?

entries.title: Arizona
entries.answer: There is more than one kind of dry landscape in Arizona. The Grand Canyon cuts through a high area of rock in the north, where some winters bring snow. Farther south, Phoenix lies in the Sonoran Desert. It can be hot there even when the high country feels cool. The Colorado River has spent a long time carving rock in Arizona. Looking at the canyon walls is one way to see that the land is built from many layers.
facts: Phoenix is the state capital, while the Grand Canyon lies much farther north.

questions.text: How did the Colorado River carve the Grand Canyon?
What large region holds the Grand Canyon?
What can you find in the rock country north of Arizona?

entries.title: Arkansas
entries.answer: Travel from the northwest of Arkansas toward the east and the terrain changes. The Ozarks have hills, valleys and clear streams. The land nearer the Mississippi River is generally flatter. Arkansas also has another set of ridges to the south of the Ozarks, the Ouachita Mountains. Little Rock, the state capital, sits on the Arkansas River. The river links mountain country and the plains as it passes through the state on its way toward the Mississippi.
facts: The Mississippi River forms much of Arkansas’s eastern boundary.

questions.text: Where are the Ozarks and what are their hills like?
Where does the Mississippi go after passing Arkansas?
What landscapes lie in Tennessee on the other side of the Mississippi?

entries.title: California
entries.answer: California stretches along much of the country’s Pacific shore, but some of its most striking places are far inland. The Central Valley sits between mountain areas and has large stretches of farmland. To its east rise the Sierra Nevada mountains. Snow and ice helped shape parts of that range, including Yosemite Valley. Farther southeast, the land also includes deserts. Sacramento, the state capital, is in the northern part of the Central Valley.
facts: The Pacific Ocean is on California’s west side.

questions.text: How did ice help shape the Sierra Nevada?
Why does Yosemite have a wide floor and steep walls?
How does the land change east of California?

entries.title: Caribbean Sea
entries.answer: The Caribbean Sea is a warm part of the Atlantic between Central America, northern South America, and a chain of islands. Cuba, Jamaica, and Hispaniola sit near its northern side. Near its eastern edge, smaller islands form a curved line with openings where water moves between the Caribbean and the wider Atlantic. The sea has deep parts, shallow reefs, and busy routes used by ships traveling between its islands and coasts.
facts: The Panama Canal links the Caribbean side of the Americas with the Pacific Ocean.

questions.text: Which country contains the canal that lets ships pass to the Pacific?
Which Central American country has a large reef offshore in the Caribbean?
Why can tropical storms grow when the ocean is warm?

entries.title: Colorado
entries.answer: In eastern Colorado, broad plains run toward the Rocky Mountains. At their foot stand Denver, the capital, and several other cities. Farther west, high mountains can hold snow even when the plains are dry. Creeks that start among those peaks do not all go toward the same ocean. A boundary known as the Continental Divide separates land that drains in different directions. To see that idea, picture drops falling on opposite sides of a roof.
facts: Colorado joined the United States in 1876.

questions.text: Where does water go on the two sides of the Rocky Mountain divide?
How do the plains change as they near the Rocky Mountains?
What landscape lies immediately west of Colorado?

entries.title: Connecticut
entries.answer: Connecticut is a small New England state on the north side of Long Island Sound. That body of water separates much of its coast from Long Island. The Connecticut River enters from the north, flows by Hartford, and reaches the sound near the state’s southeastern coast. Hartford is the capital. A traveler following the river can see how a waterway ties inland towns to a coast with salt water and tides.
facts: The Connecticut River flows through several New England states before it reaches the ocean.

questions.text: What lies between Long Island and the Connecticut coast?
Which other states are part of New England?
What is the state just north of Connecticut like?

entries.title: Delaware
entries.answer: On the map, Delaware is tucked along the eastern side of the Delmarva Peninsula. This long stretch of land is shared by parts of Delaware, Maryland and Virginia. The Delaware River and its bay lie on the other side of much of the state from Maryland. Along the coast are low sandy shores and flat wetlands. Dover, the capital, is inland from the bay. Because Delaware is small, those different pieces fit into a short drive.
facts: Delaware was the first state to approve the United States Constitution, in 1787.

questions.text: What makes the Delmarva Peninsula a peninsula?
Which neighbor shares the Delmarva Peninsula with Delaware?
Why is much of the land by Delaware’s shore so low?

entries.title: Florida
entries.answer: Most of Florida lies on a peninsula that reaches south from the rest of the United States. Its western side faces the Gulf and its eastern side faces the Atlantic Ocean. In the far south, water moves slowly through the marshes of the Everglades. Then the Florida Keys trail out into the sea in a long line. The capital, Tallahassee, is far north of those islands, near the part of Florida that extends west along the Gulf Coast.
facts: The long, narrow extension of northern Florida is often called the Panhandle.

questions.text: Why are the Everglades called a river of grass?
What lies beyond the southern tip of Florida?
How can you tell Florida is a peninsula?

entries.title: Georgia
entries.answer: Georgia’s land rises from low coastal plains in the southeast to mountains in the north. The state capital, Atlanta, sits between those ends in a hilly stretch of land called the Piedmont. The Atlantic coast includes marshes and long islands close to the shore. The Savannah River marks much of the line between Georgia and South Carolina. Two parts of Georgia can look quite different because the mountain country and the sea are far apart.
facts: The city of Savannah sits near the mouth of the Savannah River.

questions.text: How does Georgia’s coastal plain differ from its hills?
What is the state across the Savannah River like?
Why are there long islands just off some southern shores?

entries.title: Hawaii
entries.answer: Hawaii is a state made of islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. The islands began as volcanoes that rose from the ocean floor. Honolulu, the capital, is on Oʻahu. The island named Hawaiʻi is often called the Big Island so it is easier to tell it apart from the whole state. Volcanoes on that island can still change the land, while waves and streams slowly wear down the shores and valleys of older islands.
facts: Both the state and its largest island share the name Hawaii, usually spelled Hawaiʻi in the Hawaiian language.

questions.text: Where is the Hawaiian volcano that is still hidden below the water?
What do we call a group of islands?
How can a hot spot build a volcano far from a plate boundary?

entries.title: Himalayas
entries.answer: The Himalayas stretch across southern Asia and contain many of Earth’s highest mountains. They started growing when the land carrying India pushed into the land to the north. The two pieces of land were so thick that rock bent, broke, and piled up instead of simply vanishing below the surface. The land is still moving, so the range is still changing. Streams from its slopes join rivers that flow into several countries.
facts: Mount Everest is the tallest peak in the Himalayas.
Earthquakes can occur where plates keep moving and the rock gets stuck.

questions.text: Which country on the south side of the Himalayas shares Mount Everest with China?
What causes the shaking when rock slips along a break?
How did the Andes grow along the west edge of South America?

entries.title: How can a flat map show hills and valleys?
entries.answer: A topographic map shows the shape of land along with features such as rivers and roads. Many use contour lines, which trace places at the same height. Picture taking an overhead photo of a stack of paper rings of different sizes. Each ring stands for a different height on a hill. The drawn rings are flat, but together they give you clues about the hill’s shape.
facts: Topographic maps can show different levels of detail, depending on the area and the map’s scale.

questions.text: What does a single contour line tell you?
How do you measure distance on a map?
How can ice carve a U-shaped valley?

entries.title: How can contour lines show whether a slope is steep?
entries.answer: A contour line connects spots that are all at the same height. Think of climbing a hill. You cross each new line when you reach another marked height. Where the lines sit close together, you gain height in a short distance, so the slope is steep. Where those same steps in height are spread far apart, the slope is gentler. Closed rings can help show the shape of a hill.
facts: A map may tell you the difference in height between one normal contour and the next.

questions.text: What is a topographic map?
Where can you find out what map marks mean?
What does altitude measure?

entries.title: How can crossing a line change the date?
entries.answer: The International Date Line runs through the Pacific Ocean. It is a line people use to keep track of which date it is around the world. When a traveler crosses it heading west, the date moves one day ahead. In the opposite direction, the date moves one day back. The line bends in places so people on nearby islands can use the same date.
facts: The Date Line runs roughly along the line marking 180 degrees of longitude.

questions.text: Why do different places use different clock times?
Where does the world start counting longitude?
What are the lines running from pole to pole called?

entries.title: How can you measure a real distance on a map?
entries.answer: A map scale tells how much real distance a length on the map stands for. If one centimeter stands for one kilometer, a straight line three centimeters long stands for three kilometers. Many maps have a little marked bar that you can use like a ruler. A trail that twists around hills can be much longer than the straight line between its start and finish.
facts: If a copy makes a whole map larger or smaller, the printed scale bar changes along with it and still gives the right distance.

questions.text: How can a flat map show hills?
What does the key on a map explain?
Why can a world map stretch some places?

entries.title: How did moving lava help build the Columbia Plateau?
entries.answer: Parts of the inland Pacific Northwest sit on huge layers of dark rock called basalt. Long ago runny lava spread across a large area and cooled. Many separate flows made a thick pile of rock. Later, streams cut deep paths through parts of the rock. The Columbia River crosses the region. When you see dark bands on the side of a valley, you may be seeing the edges of different sheets of cooled lava.
facts: The Columbia Plateau’s layers formed across a wide area, far beyond a single volcano cone.

questions.text: What wide areas lie east of Washington’s Cascade Mountains?
What kind of rock can form when runny lava cools?
How can rivers remove pieces of rock over time?

entries.title: How did such a long inlet form in Washington?
entries.answer: Puget Sound is a long network of inlets in western Washington, connected to seawater from the Pacific Ocean. During a recent ice age, a large sheet of ice moved through the area. It scraped rock, scooped some valleys deeper and left loose material behind. When the ice melted back, seawater could fill some of the low places. The sound now has many arms and bays. Olympia lies near the southern end of the network.
facts: The hills and shorelines around Puget Sound still show traces of the ice that passed through.

questions.text: Where is Washington’s capital compared with Puget Sound?
How can a moving glacier wear away rock?
Where is another sound where fresh and salty water mix?

entries.title: How did the Mississippi build land near the Gulf?
entries.answer: As the Mississippi River slows near the Gulf Coast, some of the sand and mud in the water settles out. Over time these deposits can build low new land between the channels. In southern Louisiana, some channels reach out into the Gulf like toes on a bird’s foot. That gives part of the coastal delta its nickname. Waves, storms, sea level and changes people make to the river can affect when land grows or washes away.
facts: The Louisiana coastal delta is different from the inland region also called the Mississippi Delta.

questions.text: How does water reach Louisiana from the river’s start in Minnesota?
What major cities sit upstream of the river’s mouth?
Where is the inland region that is also called the Mississippi Delta?

entries.title: How did wind help build Iowa’s Loess Hills?
entries.answer: Along the Missouri River valley in western Iowa stand hills built of very small grains of soil called loess. During cold periods, water from melting ice carried fine bits of rock into wide river valleys. When mud on the floodplain dried, wind could lift those tiny grains and move them. The dust settled on higher land, slowly making very thick banks. Streams later cut through those banks and helped carve the steep shapes visible today.
facts: Much of the dust that built these hills came from the flat valley near the Missouri River.

questions.text: Where in Iowa are the Loess Hills?
How can moving ice scrape the ground and carry rock?
What is the flat land beside a river called?

entries.title: How do fresh and salty water meet in Chesapeake Bay?
entries.answer: Chesapeake Bay reaches inland from the Atlantic Ocean between land in Maryland and Virginia. Rivers bring fresh water into the bay. The mouth of a river, or river mouth, is where it reaches the bay. The large Susquehanna River enters near the northern end. Ocean water adds salt nearer the bay’s mouth. These waters mix, but some parts are less salty than others. That provides several kinds of habitat for plants and animals, from river mouths to the wider, saltier bay.
facts: Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States.

questions.text: How does the bay split Maryland into different-looking pieces?
What do we call a coastal place where fresh and salt water mix?
Where can you find another large estuary north of the Chesapeake?

entries.title: How do pine trees grow in the sandy Pinelands?
entries.answer: The Pinelands lie on southern New Jersey’s low coastal plain. Much of their soil is sandy, so water drains through it more easily than it does through sticky clay. Pitch pines and some other plants can grow well there even though this kind of soil holds little food for many plants. The land is not dry everywhere. Places where water is close to the surface can stay wet and support different plants and animals.
facts: The larger Pine Barrens landscape includes both pine woods and wetlands.

questions.text: Which part of New Jersey holds the Pinelands?
Why do so many parts of the coastal plain have sandy ground?
What makes some land stay wet long enough to become a wetland?

entries.title: How does a letter-and-number grid help you find a place?
entries.answer: A map grid divides a map into little squares. A row or column of letters and a row or column of numbers can give each square a name, such as B3. To find B3, follow the band marked B until you reach the band numbered 3. The grid gets you to the right area so you can look for the exact park, street, or building.
facts: A letter-and-number grid helps you search one map. Latitude and longitude can tell people where to look anywhere on Earth.

questions.text: How can you recognize a park or road symbol?
How can you measure the length of a road on the map?
How does a globe grid mark how far north a place is?

entries.title: Idaho
entries.answer: Much of Idaho is mountain country, but a wide curve of lower land runs across the south. This is the Snake River Plain. The river and nearby towns can be followed across southern Idaho on a map. Boise, the capital, stands along the Boise River near the northern side of the western plain. The wide, open country there is different from the forests and steep slopes farther north. Idaho also touches Canada at its narrow northern tip.
facts: The Snake River passes through Idaho and joins the Columbia River farther west.

questions.text: How did lava shape some of the land around the Columbia and Snake rivers?
What does the mountain country east of Idaho look like?
Where does the Snake River meet the Columbia?

entries.title: Illinois
entries.answer: Illinois has water on several edges. Chicago stands on Lake Michigan in the northeast. The Mississippi River runs along the western border, and the Ohio River reaches the state’s southern tip. Between the edges lie broad areas of gently rolling farmland. Springfield, the capital, is inland. Looking from Chicago toward Springfield helps explain why people have very different pictures in mind when they hear the name Illinois, from a city lakeshore to a wide farm field.
facts: The Ohio and Mississippi rivers meet near Cairo at the southern tip of Illinois.

questions.text: Which lake is Chicago beside?
Where does the river along western Illinois go?
What is the state across part of that river like?

entries.title: Indiana
entries.answer: Indiana touches Lake Michigan at its northwest corner, where sand dunes rise above the beach. The capital, Indianapolis, lies near the middle of the state, away from that lakeshore. Across central Indiana much of the land rolls gently. Farther south, rivers cut through hillier areas, and the Ohio River bends along much of the state’s southern edge. Visiting north and south would give two different views of what people often picture as one flat stretch of farmland.
facts: Indiana Dunes National Park protects part of the state’s Lake Michigan shore.

questions.text: How does wind build hills of sand beside a lake?
Which state lies across much of Indiana’s southern river boundary?
How does Lake Michigan fit among the Great Lakes?

entries.title: Iowa
entries.answer: Iowa sits between two major rivers, the Mississippi on the east and the Missouri along much of its western edge. Much of the land between them is gently rolling and is used to grow crops. Des Moines, the capital, is named for one of the state’s inland rivers. Along the western side, steep hills rise near the Missouri River valley. Much of the material in those hills was carried there by wind long ago.
facts: The Mississippi River separates Iowa from Illinois and Wisconsin.

questions.text: How did wind bring material to hills along the Missouri River?
How does the Mississippi connect Iowa to other places?
What is the state across much of Iowa’s western river boundary like?

entries.title: Kansas
entries.answer: The land rises gradually from eastern Kansas toward the west. Near Topeka, the capital, rivers wind through hilly areas. Farther west, long open views across the high plains make roads look as if they reach straight into the sky. In the middle of eastern Kansas are the Flint Hills, where much of the ground is too rocky for easy plowing. There are still places there where tall prairie grasses can grow.
facts: Kansas lies in the central United States between Nebraska and Oklahoma.

questions.text: Why is so much tallgrass prairie left in the Flint Hills?
How far does the broader Great Plains region reach?
How does the landscape continue north of Kansas?

entries.title: Kentucky
entries.answer: Kentucky has Appalachian hills in the east, gently rolling country around its middle and flatter river country in parts of the west. In the center, the Bluegrass region includes the state capital, Frankfort. In south-central Kentucky, water has dissolved some of the rock underground to make caves. Mammoth Cave is part of that hidden world. On the north, the Ohio River curves around Kentucky and separates it from several other states.
facts: Kentucky became a state in 1792.

questions.text: What opened so many passages underneath part of Kentucky?
Which long eastern mountain chain reaches into Kentucky?
How does the Ohio River connect Kentucky and Indiana?

entries.title: Louisiana
entries.answer: The Mississippi River curves through southern Louisiana toward the Gulf. Its wide valley and low marshes look very different from the hills in parts of the north. Over a long time the river dropped sand and mud near the coast, helping shape the land low beside the water. Baton Rouge, the capital, is upstream from New Orleans. Both cities sit near important bends of the same river at different points on its path to the sea.
facts: The Mississippi finishes its long trip through the United States in Louisiana.

questions.text: Where does the river begin before arriving in Louisiana?
How does the river leave land behind when it reaches the coast?
Which state shares part of the lower river with Louisiana?

entries.title: Maine
entries.answer: Maine is at the northeastern end of New England. Inland, forests cover a large part of the state and Mount Katahdin rises above nearby lakes and wooded valleys. On the Atlantic side, bays, islands and rocky points make the coastline twist and turn on a map. Augusta, the capital, is on the Kennebec River, away from the open coast. Acadia National Park includes stretches where waves reach the base of rocky, wooded land.
facts: Maine is the only U.S. state that borders just one other state, New Hampshire.

questions.text: Where can you see Maine’s rocky headlands in a national park?
Which other New England states lie south of Maine?
What is Maine’s only U.S. state neighbor like?

entries.title: Maryland
entries.answer: The Chesapeake Bay almost splits Maryland into separate pieces on a map. The Eastern Shore lies between the bay and the Atlantic coast. Annapolis, the capital, is on the west side of the bay near the mouth of the Severn River. If you keep traveling west, you can leave the low shore behind and reach the mountains. That makes Maryland a place where both wide water views and wooded mountain slopes are part of one state.
facts: Fresh river water and salty sea water mix in Chesapeake Bay.

questions.text: How do fresh and salty water meet in Chesapeake Bay?
What big chain includes mountains in western Maryland?
What is Maryland’s neighbor on the Delmarva Peninsula like?

entries.title: Massachusetts
entries.answer: Massachusetts has an Atlantic coast in the east and rolling hills and mountains in the west. Boston, the capital, grew around a harbor. Southeast of Boston, Cape Cod curves out into the water like a bent arm. The Connecticut River crosses the western part of the state and cuts a wider, lower valley between uplands. The wide valley, sandy cape and busy harbor are three very different places on a map of one state.
facts: Boston Harbor was the setting of the Boston Tea Party in 1773.

questions.text: How did Cape Cod get its long, sandy shape?
What happened in Boston Harbor during the protest?
What group of states includes Massachusetts?

entries.title: Michigan
entries.answer: Michigan has two big sections of land, called the Upper and Lower peninsulas. The Lower Peninsula is famous for looking a little like a mitten on a map. By road, the Mackinac Bridge carries travelers between the two parts. Lakes surround so much of Michigan that water looks almost as important as land on a map of it. Lansing, the capital, lies inland in the Lower Peninsula.
facts: Michigan touches four Great Lakes, all except Lake Ontario.

questions.text: What are the names of all five Great Lakes?
What makes both large parts of Michigan peninsulas?
Which state shares a land border with the Upper Peninsula?

entries.title: Minnesota
entries.answer: Minnesota has forests and many lakes in the north, more farmland toward the south and west, and a part of Lake Superior on its northeastern edge. The Mississippi River begins at Lake Itasca and winds across the state before turning south. Farther down that river sits Saint Paul, the capital, next to Minneapolis. Those cities are often called the Twin Cities. They are much farther downstream than the quiet outlet where the Mississippi starts.
facts: You can find both the start of the Mississippi and a shore of Lake Superior in Minnesota.

questions.text: Where does the Mississippi travel after it leaves northern Minnesota?
How large is Superior compared with the other Great Lakes?
What is the state just east of Minnesota like?

entries.title: Mississippi
entries.answer: Mississippi reaches from the lower Mississippi River valley to the Gulf Coast. The western side includes low, flat land by the river. The center and east have some rolling higher country, and sandy shores and marshes appear near the Gulf. Jackson is the capital. In the state, a region often called the Mississippi Delta is inland in the northwest. It is different from the river’s mouth and coastal delta in Louisiana.
facts: The Mississippi River forms much of the state’s western edge.

questions.text: What long trip takes the river to Mississippi?
Where is the river’s coastal delta?
What is Mississippi’s eastern neighbor like?

entries.title: Missouri
entries.answer: The Missouri River crosses the state from west to east and joins the Mississippi near St. Louis. Jefferson City, the capital, stands by the Missouri River near the center of the state. To the south, the Ozarks have rounded hills and valleys with streams and springs. Farther north, the land is often lower and more gently rolling. Missouri’s two main rivers help explain where several of its larger towns grew.
facts: Missouri is the name of both a state and a river that crosses it.

questions.text: Why are the Ozarks hillier than nearby plains?
Which rivers flow into the Mississippi?
Which state lies just west of Missouri?

entries.title: Montana
entries.answer: Montana has steep mountains in its west and broad, more open plains toward its east. Helena, the state capital, sits in the western part of the state. The plains are part of a much larger region that stretches across the center of North America. Montana’s northern edge touches Canada, and the northern Rocky Mountains continue across that line. So the straight border on the map does not mark a sudden change in the landscape.
facts: Glacier National Park protects mountain country in northwestern Montana.

questions.text: Where do the open plains in eastern Montana continue?
What country lies north of Montana?
What is the mountain state across much of Montana’s western edge like?

entries.title: Nebraska
entries.answer: Nebraska stretches west from the Missouri River into the Great Plains. Lincoln, its capital, is near the eastern end. A traveler going west can pass wide farmland, the long path of the Platte River and an area of grass-covered dunes called the Sandhills. Those hills can look green instead of sandy because grasses grow on top of the sand. The western end of Nebraska is higher than much of the east.
facts: The Platte River flows east across Nebraska and joins the Missouri River.

questions.text: Why don’t the Nebraska Sandhills look like a bare desert?
How does Nebraska fit into the wider Great Plains?
Which state is across the Missouri River from eastern Nebraska?

entries.title: Nevada
entries.answer: Nevada has many mountain ranges with long, lower valleys between them. Much of the state is in the Great Basin, where rain and snowmelt collect inland instead of flowing to the sea. The state capital, Carson City, is in western Nevada near the Sierra Nevada. Las Vegas is far to the south in a different desert setting. Both sit in a dry state, but there is a long trip between them.
facts: On a map Nevada has a long diagonal line where much of its border with California runs.

questions.text: Why does so much water in Nevada stay away from the sea?
What mountains are near Nevada’s western edge?
What lies west of Nevada’s diagonal border?

entries.title: New Hampshire
entries.answer: New Hampshire includes high mountains, lake country, wooded river valleys and a short Atlantic coast. The White Mountains lie well north of the capital, Concord, and include Mount Washington. Much of the western edge follows the Connecticut River, with Vermont on the other side. Near the southeast corner, the state reaches the sea. The mountains can get much colder weather than the coast, even though both are in one small state.
facts: Mount Washington is the highest peak in New Hampshire.

questions.text: What other states are in the same region as New Hampshire?
What is the state on the other side of the Connecticut River like?
What kinds of shores does the state to the east have?

entries.title: New Jersey
entries.answer: New Jersey lies between the Delaware River and the Atlantic Ocean. Trenton, the capital, is on the river across from Pennsylvania. Parts of northern New Jersey are close to New York City, but farther south the landscape can be much more open. The Pinelands have forests, sandy soil and wetlands. On the Atlantic side, long sandy islands shelter some quieter waters from the open sea.
facts: The Delaware River forms much of New Jersey’s western border.

questions.text: How do pine trees grow in the sandy Pinelands?
What lies behind the long islands on New Jersey’s coast?
What is the state across the Delaware River from Trenton like?

entries.title: New Mexico
entries.answer: New Mexico stretches from mountains in the north to dry plains and valleys farther south. Santa Fe, the state capital, sits high above sea level in the northern part of the state. The Rio Grande flows south past Albuquerque. Farther south, White Sands looks like a field of snow from a distance, although its dunes are made of a mineral called gypsum. The high ground helps explain why some parts of New Mexico can be cool even on a clear day.
facts: New Mexico shares part of its southern border with Mexico.

questions.text: Why are the dunes at White Sands so white?
What does it mean for a place to stand high above sea level?
What is the state just west of New Mexico like?

entries.title: New York
entries.answer: New York City sits at the southern end of the state, where the Hudson River reaches tidal waters and a busy harbor. Far upriver, Albany is the state capital. A traveler going north can reach the Adirondack Mountains. To the west, the state touches two Great Lakes and reaches Niagara Falls. Looking at all those places together shows why New York State has many kinds of landscapes far beyond its best-known city.
facts: New York touches Lake Erie and Lake Ontario.

questions.text: What can you find north of Albany in the Adirondacks?
Which of the Great Lakes meet New York State?
Why did builders dig a water route across New York?

entries.title: Nile River
entries.answer: The Nile flows north through northeastern Africa to the Mediterranean. The Blue Nile carries water from Ethiopia, and the White Nile brings water from areas farther south. The two meet at Khartoum in Sudan. Downstream, the river crosses some very dry country. Near the sea, branches spread across a delta built in part from mud the river carried. That mud can make good soil for farmers.
facts: The Nile reaches the Mediterranean on Egypt’s coast.
The Nile flows north even though many people picture rivers as flowing south on a map.

questions.text: Which country carries the Blue Nile from the Ethiopian highlands?
In which country does the Nile form a delta at the Mediterranean?
Which South American river carries even more water into the ocean?

entries.title: North Carolina
entries.answer: North Carolina runs from the mountains in the west to the Atlantic in the east. Between them are rolling hills where Raleigh, the capital, is located. At the coast, the Outer Banks are long sandy islands separated from much of the mainland by wide, protected waters. In the opposite direction, the Great Smoky Mountains straddle the state line with Tennessee. That long distance from mountains to sea gives people many different kinds of places to explore.
facts: The Outer Banks lie seaward of large bodies of water called sounds.

questions.text: Why do the Outer Banks form long, narrow islands?
Why does the mountain country shared with Tennessee look smoky from a distance?
What does North Carolina’s western neighbor look like?

entries.title: North Dakota
entries.answer: North Dakota lies in the northern Great Plains. The Missouri River flows past Bismarck, the state capital. In the west, the Little Missouri River and smaller streams have cut steep-sided valleys into layers of rock, making part of the badlands. Much farther east, the broad Red River valley is much flatter. Those two areas show how different the plains can look across one state. The northern border meets Canada.
facts: North Dakota’s neighbor to the south is South Dakota.

questions.text: Where do the broad plains reach beyond North Dakota?
Why do some plains hold bunches of steep ravines?
What does the state just south of North Dakota look like?

entries.title: Ohio
entries.answer: Ohio has a Great Lake on one side and a large river on another. To the north, cities such as Cleveland grew beside Lake Erie. The Ohio River curves along much of the south and east. Columbus, the capital, is inland near the middle of the state. Parts of western Ohio have broad, fairly flat land. The southeastern hills belong to the western side of the long Appalachian region.
facts: Lake Erie separates part of northern Ohio from Canada, with an international border in the lake.

questions.text: Where is Lake Erie among the Great Lakes?
What long area of mountains and plateaus reaches toward southeastern Ohio?
Which neighbor lies across much of Ohio’s southeastern river boundary?

entries.title: Oklahoma
entries.answer: Oklahoma spreads from flatter, drier land in the west to hills and forests toward its east. A long strip called the Panhandle reaches out at the northwest. Oklahoma City, the capital, sits much closer to the center. Two rivers also help with orientation. The Arkansas River passes through the northeast, and the Red River makes most of the southern boundary with Texas. Looking at both rivers shows the state has several different water routes.
facts: Oklahoma’s Panhandle touches New Mexico at its western end.

questions.text: What larger plains region reaches into western Oklahoma?
What lies across the Red River from Oklahoma?
What land lies west of Oklahoma’s Panhandle?

entries.title: Oregon
entries.answer: Oregon’s Pacific coast has cliffs, beaches and forested headlands. Inland from the coast are valleys, including the Willamette Valley where Salem, the capital, is located. The Cascade Range rises farther east. Near its southern part in Oregon, Crater Lake fills a large hollow left by a volcano. Beyond the Cascades, parts of eastern Oregon are much drier and more open than the green country on the west side.
facts: The Columbia River forms much of the border between Oregon and Washington.

questions.text: Why do so many volcanoes rise in the Cascade Range?
How did a volcano help form Crater Lake?
What lies across the Columbia River from much of northern Oregon?

entries.title: Pennsylvania
entries.answer: Pennsylvania’s middle has long ridges with valleys between them, part of the Appalachian region. Harrisburg, the capital, stands on the Susquehanna River in that part of the state. Farther east, Philadelphia lies along the Delaware River. To the west, three rivers meet at Pittsburgh: the Allegheny and Monongahela join to form the Ohio. Those separate river routes help explain why towns grew in different places as people traveled and moved goods.
facts: A short part of Pennsylvania touches Lake Erie in the northwest.

questions.text: Why are so many long mountain ridges found in the eastern United States?
Where does the Susquehanna River go after passing Pennsylvania?
What important meeting took place in Philadelphia in 1787?

entries.title: Rhode Island
entries.answer: Rhode Island is the smallest U.S. state by area. The ocean makes it look complicated on a map anyway. Narragansett Bay reaches far inland, with several islands in it. Providence, the capital, is near the head of the bay. Some parts of the state are on the mainland, while others are on islands. That is why the name can be confusing if you expect the whole state to be a single island.
facts: The Atlantic Ocean lies south of Rhode Island.

questions.text: Which other states share the same New England region?
What lies west of Rhode Island?
What is the name for several islands grouped together?

entries.title: Sahara Desert
entries.answer: The Sahara is a huge dry region that stretches across northern Africa from the Atlantic side toward the Red Sea. Its landscape includes flat rocky areas, mountains, patches of dunes, and places where water helps people and plants survive. A patch of dunes can move as wind piles sand on one side and lets it fall on the other. Much of the desert is so dry that plants grow far apart.
facts: The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth.
A desert is defined by how dry it is, so deserts can also be cold.

questions.text: Which North African country contains a large stretch of the Sahara south of its coast?
Which large river crosses the dry eastern part of the Sahara?
How do wind and water carry rock and sand from one place to another?

entries.title: South Carolina
entries.answer: South Carolina slopes from higher land in the northwest toward the Atlantic Ocean. Columbia, the capital, lies inland where rivers pass between the hilly country and lower plains. Near the coast, a broad area called the Lowcountry has salt marshes, tidal streams and islands. Charleston is on a harbor there. The rise from marshes toward wooded hills can be gradual, so a map of rivers and land height helps show the change.
facts: Part of South Carolina reaches the Blue Ridge Mountains in its far northwest.

questions.text: What broad area includes South Carolina’s Lowcountry?
What mountain country touches the far northwest of the state?
What is the state across much of the Savannah River like?

entries.title: South Dakota
entries.answer: Eastern South Dakota has open country shaped in part by past glaciers. The Missouri River passes the capital, Pierre, and divides much of the state into eastern and western parts. In the west, the Black Hills rise above the surrounding plains. Nearby badlands have sharply cut hills and gullies where rock layers are easy to see. They look quite different from each other even though both are in the western part of the same state.
facts: The Missouri River flows through both North Dakota and South Dakota.

questions.text: Why can you see bands of different colors in the badlands?
Why do the Black Hills stand out from the surrounding plains?
What land lies just north of South Dakota?

entries.title: Tennessee
entries.answer: Tennessee is long from west to east. The Mississippi River runs beside its western end near Memphis, but the eastern end rises into the Appalachian Mountains. Nashville, the capital, is in the middle part of the state on the Cumberland River. Near the far eastern edge, the Great Smoky Mountains rise along the North Carolina border. A drive across Tennessee goes through many landscapes without needing to go far north or south.
facts: Tennessee touches eight other states.

questions.text: Where do Tennessee and North Carolina share mountain country?
What passes Memphis on its way toward the Gulf?
What is the state just north of much of Tennessee like?

entries.title: Texas
entries.answer: Texas stretches from low shores on the Gulf to high, dry country in the west. Austin, the state capital, is in central Texas along a river called the Colorado. That river is separate from the Colorado River that carved the Grand Canyon. The Rio Grande forms much of the boundary with Mexico and turns around a large bend in far western Texas. These different rivers and their valleys help divide Texas into very different-looking parts.
facts: Texas has the largest area of any U.S. state apart from Alaska.

questions.text: Where does the Rio Grande begin before reaching Texas?
Which state shares part of the Rio Grande above Texas?
What kind of land is found along much of the Texas shore?

entries.title: Utah
entries.answer: Utah has several very different kinds of land. On the west are dry valleys and separate mountain ranges. In the north, mountains rise above the Great Salt Lake, near Salt Lake City, the capital. Southern and eastern Utah contain much of the Colorado Plateau, where rock layers show in canyons and natural arches. The divide between these regions is part of what makes Utah’s landscape change quickly on a long drive.
facts: The Great Salt Lake has no river outlet to the ocean.

questions.text: Why does water in some western valleys stay inland?
How did so many natural arches form in Utah?
What wider rock country stretches across much of southern Utah?

entries.title: Vermont
entries.answer: Vermont takes its name from words meaning green mountain. The Green Mountains run roughly north to south through the state. To their west, several towns sit near the broad water of Lake Champlain, with New York on the other side. To their east, the Connecticut River marks much of the edge beside New Hampshire. Montpelier, the capital, is inland among hills and valleys rather than on either of those outer edges.
facts: This New England state touches Canada at the north.

questions.text: What other states make up the New England region?
What mountain state lies across the Connecticut River?
What state lies across much of Lake Champlain?

entries.title: Virginia
entries.answer: Virginia reaches from the Atlantic and Chesapeake Bay in the east to Appalachian ridges in the west. Richmond, the capital, sits on the James River where the river passes from higher ground onto the lower coastal plain. West of Richmond, gentle hills lead toward the Blue Ridge Mountains. Near the southeastern shore, several rivers and bays give ships routes between inland water and the Atlantic Ocean.
facts: The James River flows past Richmond toward Chesapeake Bay.

questions.text: Where does the James River meet saltier ocean water?
What high country lies west of Virginia’s hills?
What mountain country lies beyond Virginia’s western border?

entries.title: Washington
entries.answer: Washington State sits in the northwest of the United States, with the Pacific Ocean to the west and Canada to the north. Olympia, the capital, is at the southern end of Puget Sound, a large inlet connected to sea water. The Cascade Range runs across the state from north to south. East of the mountains are wide, often drier areas. The Snake River joins the Columbia in the southeastern part of the state.
facts: Washington State and Washington, D.C., are on opposite sides of the country.

questions.text: How did such a long inlet form near Olympia?
What mountains separate wetter and drier parts of Washington?
What lies across the Columbia River from much of southern Washington?
Where is the country’s capital compared with Washington State?

entries.title: West Virginia
entries.answer: West Virginia sits within the Appalachian region. Its mountains, high plateaus and deep river valleys give it a very uneven landscape. Charleston, the state capital, stands where the Elk River meets the Kanawha. Farther southeast, the New River runs through a deep, wooded gorge. Along much of the northwest, the Ohio River divides West Virginia from Ohio. On a flat map its borders can look puzzling, but some follow the twists of watercourses.
facts: West Virginia became a separate state in 1863.

questions.text: What larger region includes West Virginia’s hills and high plateaus?
Why is the New River far below the land around it?
What state lies across much of the Ohio River from West Virginia?

entries.title: What are the continents?
entries.answer: Continents are Earth’s biggest regions of land. A common way to name them uses seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. The list is a way people organize the map. Europe and Asia, for example, share one large stretch of land. Some maps group the two together as Eurasia. Continents are much larger than most countries. Africa holds many countries, while a common school map uses the name Australia for both a country and the smallest continent.
facts: Antarctica surrounds the South Pole.
Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, and South America each include many countries.

questions.text: What is the country of Australia like?
Which large country covers much of North America?
Why are continents stretched on some types of maps?

entries.title: What can you find in New York’s Adirondack Mountains?
entries.answer: The Adirondack Mountains are in the northern part of New York State. On a map the high land looks like a wide raised patch rather than one very long line of peaks. Much of its rock is ancient. High peaks, wooded slopes, lakes and wetlands are all part of the region today. The Adirondack Park includes both land cared for by the state and land owned by other people, so there are towns within its broad boundary.
facts: The High Peaks area includes some of the tallest mountains in New York.

questions.text: What other kinds of land or water are in New York State?
How can a flat map show the Adirondacks’ high peaks?
What is the state across Lake Champlain like?

entries.title: What do mapmakers choose to show?
entries.answer: A mapmaker collects information about places and decides which details a map should show. A map for a park visitor might mark trails and restrooms. A map for a bus rider might skip most trails and make bus stops easy to spot. Mapmakers can use measurements from the ground and pictures taken from above. They choose labels and symbols to make the map readable, then change it when the information needs updating.
facts: A person who makes maps is also called a cartographer.

questions.text: Who measures locations on the ground?
Why do public buses stop at regular places?
Who plans work such as bridges and roads?

entries.title: What does a map legend tell you?
entries.answer: A map legend is a guide to the marks and colors on a map. A blue line might show a stream, while a different line might show a road or a border. The same symbol can mean different things on two kinds of maps, so check the legend before guessing. A useful map marks just the features that help its reader, such as trails on a park map.
facts: A map legend is often called a key.

questions.text: How do you tell how far apart places are on a map?
What can brown lines on some maps show?
What kinds of details does a topographic map show?

entries.title: What is a strait?
entries.answer: A strait is a narrow stretch of water that links two larger bodies of water. It lies between pieces of land. For example, the Strait of Gibraltar links the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. A strait can matter to people who move goods by ship because it may offer a short way from one sea into another. Most straits are natural passages.
facts: A canal is a waterway people make or change to let water or boats pass. A strait generally forms naturally.

questions.text: What do you call a narrow strip of land between two bodies of water?
How did a human-made passage change ocean travel?
Why are some coastal cities ports?

entries.title: What is an archipelago?
entries.answer: An archipelago is a group of islands. Some groups make a long chain and others look like scattered dots on a map. Islands in a chain can be peaks of volcanoes that rose above the water. A group of islands can also have another beginning, such as coral growing in shallow water over time. Islands in the same group may differ in size, shape, and wildlife.
facts: The Galápagos Islands are an archipelago in the Pacific Ocean.

questions.text: What makes the Galápagos Islands special?
What is different about a peninsula?
How do small animals build coral reefs?

entries.title: What is an isthmus?
entries.answer: An isthmus is a narrow piece of land that connects two larger pieces of land, with water on both sides. Look for the narrow spot of Panama between the wider lands of North and South America. That land was a barrier for boats that needed to get from one ocean to the other. People built a canal across it so ships could take a shorter route.
facts: A trail across an isthmus follows land. A strait is a passage through water.

questions.text: How did the Panama Canal change a ship’s journey?
How can a piece of land stick out into water and still meet the mainland?
How does a canal lock move a boat up or down?

entries.title: What is latitude?
entries.answer: Latitude tells you how far north or south a place is from Earth’s equator. Imagine putting a belt around the middle of a globe. That belt marks zero degrees of latitude. A place north of the belt has a north latitude, and a place south of it has a south latitude. Lines of equal latitude run around the globe like rings, getting smaller near the poles. Many places share one latitude. To find a single point, you also need its longitude.

sections.heading: Try a globe
sections.text: Pick a point on the globe and trace sideways along its latitude line. You may pass through several countries without ever moving north or south.

facts: The North Pole is at 90 degrees north latitude.
The equator is at zero degrees latitude.

questions.text: What does the other number in a pair of coordinates tell you?
What divides Earth into a north half and a south half?
Why are parallel lines drawn differently on different world maps?

quiz.question: Which number tells you how far north a place is?
quiz.explanation: Latitude measures position north or south of the equator.

entries.title: What is longitude?
entries.answer: Longitude tells you how far east or west a place is from the line chosen as zero longitude. This starting line is called the prime meridian. Longitude lines meet at the North and South poles. Picture the seams between slices of an orange going from its top to its bottom. If you only know a place’s longitude, it could be anywhere along one line. Put longitude together with latitude to give an address that works even in the middle of an ocean.

sections.heading: A shared starting line
sections.text: People once used several different starting lines on their maps. In 1884, an international meeting chose the line used at the Greenwich observatory in London as the common reference.

facts: Longitude is measured in degrees.
Longitude lines meet at both poles.

questions.text: What tells you whether a place lies north or south?
What does the zero line for latitude circle?
How do mapmakers fit a globe’s lines onto flat paper?

entries.title: What is the prime meridian?
entries.answer: A meridian is an imagined line between the North Pole and South Pole. The prime meridian is the line given the number zero so people can measure how far east or west places are. It runs through the Greenwich area of London in the United Kingdom. The zero line plays a role like the first mark on a ruler, although the measurements here are made in degrees.
facts: The line on the opposite side of Earth is at 180 degrees longitude.

questions.text: How do degrees of longitude tell you where a place is?
Which line helps us measure north and south?
How can travelers cross into a different date?

entries.title: What kind of land stretches along the Gulf Coast?
entries.answer: Along much of the Gulf Coast of the United States, low land reaches inland from the shore. It is part of a coastal plain built from sand, mud and other material carried and dropped by water over long periods. Some parts have forests or farms. Near the coast, where the land is almost level, slow rivers, bays and marshes are common. Farther inland, the plain gradually meets higher ground. Its width and exact edge vary from place to place.
facts: The low land along the Gulf is part of a larger coastal plain that continues along much of the Atlantic coast.

questions.text: Why is so much of southern Louisiana low and wet?
How can a river build land where it reaches the coast?
What is the low plain like along the Atlantic coast?

entries.title: What lies between Connecticut and Long Island?
entries.answer: Long Island Sound is an arm of water between the north shore of Long Island and the mainland coasts of Connecticut and part of New York. At its eastern end, water can move between the sound and the Atlantic Ocean. Rivers bring in fresh water, while tides bring in salt water from the sea. The two kinds of water mix. Bays, marshes and river mouths around the sound give fish and birds several kinds of places to live.
facts: Long Island Sound is an estuary, a coastal area where fresh river water and salty ocean water mix.

questions.text: Which state runs along much of the north side of the sound?
What can happen when river water meets salt water?
What other large estuary lies farther south?

entries.title: What makes a city a port?
entries.answer: A port is a place where boats or ships can stop to load or unload people or goods. Some ports are along the ocean and others sit beside rivers or lakes. Many ships tie up at a dock, where workers can lift boxes or roll goods onto land. Trains and trucks may carry those goods farther from the water. A city can grow near a port because many people work and trade there.
facts: The Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway connect ports far inland with the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.text: Which lakes are linked to the Atlantic Ocean?
What is the difference between goods sent away and goods brought in?
What is a narrow water passage between seas?

entries.title: What makes a plateau different from a mountain peak?
entries.answer: A plateau is a high area of land with a broad, fairly level top. A single sharp mountain peak comes to a much smaller point. Rivers can cut deep valleys across a plateau over a long time, leaving level parts of land high on either side. As you look across one of those valleys, the high land on both sides may look almost like one tabletop cut into pieces.
facts: The Colorado Plateau is a large high region that includes the Grand Canyon.

questions.text: How did the Grand Canyon become so deep?
How can water slowly carve solid rock?
What shapes rise from a plateau in Türkiye?

entries.title: What makes the Ozarks hillier than nearby plains?
entries.answer: The Ozarks spread across parts of Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma and nearby Kansas. In much of the region, the land is high enough for streams to cut downward and leave steep valleys between the hills. Water can also seep into cracks in some rock, including limestone. That moving water helps form caves and can appear again in springs. The Current and Jacks Fork rivers in Missouri pass through country where springs feed cold, clear water into the streams.
facts: The Ozarks have plateaus as well as steep-sided valleys.

questions.text: Where are the Ozarks in Arkansas?
How can water underground come out of the ground naturally?
How can streams carve valleys into a high area of land?

entries.title: What shaped the Sierra Nevada mountains?
entries.answer: The Sierra Nevada is a long mountain range mainly in eastern California, along the western side of Nevada. Large bodies of rock, including granite, make up many of its high slopes. Movement in Earth’s rocky outer layer helped lift the range. Later, glaciers scraped away rock and widened some valleys. You can see the result at Yosemite, where a broad valley lies below steep rock walls. Streams and weather still wear down the range today.
facts: Mount Whitney is one of the range’s tallest landmarks and the highest mountain in the 48 connected U.S. states.

questions.text: What helped give Yosemite Valley its steep walls?
How can a slow-moving glacier scrape rock?
What other landscapes are west of the Sierra Nevada?

entries.title: When is a piece of land called a peninsula?
entries.answer: A peninsula sticks out into water but stays joined to a larger piece of land. Most of Florida reaches out between the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico, and a road can take you there without crossing either sea. Peninsulas come in different sizes. On a map, you can look for the place where water runs along the edges and a solid stretch of land still connects to the rest.
facts: A peninsula is still connected to other land, while an island is surrounded by water.

questions.text: What do we call a narrow piece of land joining two larger ones?
What do we call a whole group of islands?
Which large lakes sit near the U.S. and Canada border?

entries.title: Where do the Appalachian Mountains run?
entries.answer: The Appalachian Mountains form a long, old group of mountain ranges in eastern North America. Their ridges, valleys and high plateaus reach from eastern Canada into the southern United States. More than one range belongs to this group, including the Blue Ridge. Movements in Earth’s rocky outer layer helped raise and fold parts of the land long ago. Over time streams and weather wore those mountains down and helped make rounded tops and long valleys.
facts: Many Appalachian ridges run in the same general direction even when valleys separate them.

questions.text: Which part of the Appalachians stretches across Virginia and North Carolina?
What does the Appalachian country look like in West Virginia?
How do wind and water carry away rock and soil?

entries.title: Where does the Mississippi River begin and end?
entries.answer: The Mississippi River begins where water flows out of Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota. It is small at first, but it gathers water from many other streams and rivers on its way south. Among the rivers that flow into it are the Missouri and the Ohio. The Mississippi passes cities such as Saint Paul, St. Louis, Memphis and New Orleans. After reaching southern Louisiana, it spreads into separate channels and meets the Gulf.
facts: Some states use part of the river’s twisting course as a border.

questions.text: Where in Minnesota does the Mississippi start?
What happens where the Mississippi empties into the sea?
Why do small streams join larger rivers?

entries.title: Where does the Rio Grande go after leaving the mountains?
entries.answer: The Rio Grande begins in the Rocky Mountains of southern Colorado. It flows into New Mexico, passing places such as Albuquerque. Farther downstream, part of the river forms the border between Texas and Mexico. It bends around the Texas area known as Big Bend on its way toward the Gulf Coast. Like other long rivers, its water and speed can change with snow, rain and the amount of water people use along the way.
facts: The river is also called the Río Bravo or Río Bravo del Norte in Mexico.

questions.text: What land makes up Colorado near the river’s headwaters?
What does the Rio Grande pass in New Mexico?
How do different rivers divide the landscape in Texas?

entries.title: Where does water go on the two sides of the Rocky Mountain divide?
entries.answer: In Rocky Mountain National Park, the high ridge known as the Continental Divide sends rain and melted snow along very different routes. Streams on the west side of the ridge feed the Colorado River. Streams on the east side join rivers that eventually reach the Mississippi. Two drops can land close together near the top of the ridge, then join streams that take them far apart as they flow downhill.
facts: A drainage divide is high ground that separates land where water flows into different rivers or lakes.

questions.text: How can you tell where the streams of one watershed lead?
How can several streams join one river?
How can a map help you see high ground and valleys?

entries.title: Where is Hawaii’s hidden undersea volcano?
entries.answer: South of the Big Island of Hawaiʻi, an active volcano called Kamaʻehuakanaloa rises from the bottom of the Pacific. Its top is still far below the water. It is part of the same volcanic chain as Hawaiʻi, Maui, Oʻahu and Kauaʻi. Many volcanoes in that chain become older as you travel northwest. The hidden volcano is near its younger southeastern end, where a volcanic hot spot can feed molten rock from deep underground. It shows that some mountains in the Hawaiian chain never appear above the waves.
facts: Kamaʻehuakanaloa was once called Lōʻihi Seamount.

questions.text: On which island is Hawaii’s capital?
How does a hot spot help form a line of volcanoes?
What do we call a group of islands above the water?

entries.title: Where is the equator?
entries.answer: The equator is an imaginary circle around Earth halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. It divides Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere. A hemisphere is half of a ball, so you can picture cutting a globe into two pieces along that line. The equator is the starting place for measuring latitude. If you crossed it by boat or on a road, you would normally need a map or a sign to know when you had passed from one side to the other.
facts: The equator is at zero degrees latitude.
The equator crosses water as well as land.

questions.text: Which East African country has land on both sides of the equator?
Which South American country’s Amazon region crosses the equator?
How do we describe places north and south of that circle?

entries.title: Which lakes make up the Great Lakes?
entries.answer: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario are the five Great Lakes in North America. They are huge bodies of fresh water, and water moves between them through connected rivers and waterways. Four of the five touch both the United States and Canada. Lake Michigan lies entirely within the United States. The linked waterway lets some ships travel inland from the Atlantic through the St. Lawrence Seaway.
facts: The Great Lakes hold fresh water, even though someone standing on a shore may not see across them.

questions.text: How can water in a large lake help make snow?
Why did people build a canal across New York?
How do inland water routes help some cities become ports?

entries.title: Which part of the Appalachians is called the Blue Ridge?
entries.answer: The Blue Ridge is one part of the longer Appalachian system in the eastern United States. Its mountains run across states including Virginia and North Carolina, and reach into nearby states. Many ridges have rounded, wooded tops. Between them, streams flow down through low gaps and valleys. On a clear day, far ridges may look bluish because light travels through a great deal of air before it reaches your eyes. The nearest slopes often look greener and sharper.
facts: The Blue Ridge contains some of the highest mountains in the eastern United States.

questions.text: Where does the longer chain containing the Blue Ridge go?
How do the Blue Ridge and coastal plain fit into Virginia?
Why do nearby mountains often look smoky?

entries.title: Which six states make up New England?
entries.answer: New England is a region in the far northeastern United States. It includes Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont. A lot changes within those six states. Five have a seacoast, while Vermont is inland beside Lake Champlain. Mountains reach across parts of northern New England. Farther south there are busy ports and much lower land. The region’s name helps group its states, but one scene does not show what all of them are like.
facts: New England includes both the United States’ smallest state, Rhode Island, and Maine, the largest state in the region by area.

entries.title: Why did one part of Wisconsin keep its steep valleys?
entries.answer: Much of Wisconsin was covered by moving ice during recent ice ages. Part of the southwest was mostly outside those ice sheets. There, rivers had a long time to cut valleys between high ridges without recent glaciers passing over them and spreading layers of loose rock. This land is called the Driftless Area, after the loose material called glacial drift that ice or its meltwater can leave behind. The wider region also reaches into neighboring states.
facts: The Driftless Area can have steep valleys close to much flatter land that was shaped by ice.

entries.title: Why do clocks show different times in different places?
entries.answer: Earth spins about once a day. When the Sun is high over one part of Earth, another part can be dark. Many places set their clocks so that noon is roughly around the bright middle of their day. They do this by using time zones, or areas that agree on a clock time. Borders of those zones can bend so that neighbors use the same clock.
facts: Some places differ from nearby zones by half an hour, and clock rules can change from place to place.

questions.text: Where can crossing a line change the date?

entries.title: Why do flat maps stretch Earth?
entries.answer: The surface of Earth curves, but paper is flat. Any way of drawing that curved surface on a flat page changes something about the places on it. One map might show the sizes of countries clearly but bend or stretch their shapes. Another map might help someone follow a steady direction at sea but make land near the poles look much bigger than it is. A map projection is a method for making that flat picture. Mapmakers choose one that works for the task at hand.

sections.heading: Compare two views
sections.text: Find a place near the top of a Mercator world map and compare its size on a globe. This kind of map stretches areas near the poles much more than it stretches areas near the equator.

facts: A globe keeps the curved shape of Earth.
An equal-area projection is designed to keep area comparisons accurate.

questions.text: Which line circles the middle of the globe?

quiz.question: Why can two world maps show the same country at different relative sizes?
options: One map changed the country’s borders overnight
Flattening a globe can stretch areas
quiz.explanation: Different projections handle the curve differently. Some preserve area comparisons, while others stretch certain places.

entries.title: Why do little streams join larger rivers?
entries.answer: A tributary is a stream or river that flows into a bigger stream or river. As water runs downhill, small streams often meet and make a larger flow. Look at a river map and you may see a pattern like the branches of a tree. Some little branches join bigger branches, and the bigger ones meet the main river. The land that drains to a common place is called a watershed.
facts: Where two streams meet, water can continue downstream in one channel.

Why can a river spread beyond its channel?

entries.title: Why do some plains hold bunches of steep ravines?
entries.answer: In places called badlands, rain and streams have cut many small, steep valleys into soft layers of rock or dirt. Rain may be rare at times, but a shower can run off quickly where few plants cover the ground. The water cuts channels and carries loose grains away. Some layers wear away faster than others, giving the hills sharp edges. Examples in both North Dakota and South Dakota show bands of different colors from different layers.
facts: Some rocks in these landscapes hold fossils, which erosion can uncover.

questions.text: Where can you see badlands in North Dakota?
How do the badlands and Black Hills fit into South Dakota?

entries.title: Why do the Black Hills stand out from the surrounding plains?
entries.answer: The Black Hills rise like an island of hills and low mountains above the plains of western South Dakota and eastern Wyoming. Long ago, rock was pushed upward. Weather and streams wore away some of the rocks that once covered the higher ground. In places the older rock below is now visible. Many slopes grow dark green pine trees, so the hills can look almost black from far away against the lighter plains.
facts: Though most of the Black Hills are in South Dakota, some extend into Wyoming.

entries.title: Why do the Florida Keys form a curved chain?
entries.answer: The Florida Keys are a line of low islands that curves away from the southern end of Florida. Many of the islands are made of limestone left by sea life long ago. The former shapes of reefs and sandy banks helped decide where islands appeared when the water was lower. There are now channels between the islands, so the land appears as a curved string of pieces on a map. Living coral reefs grow offshore on the Atlantic side.
facts: A key is a low island, and there are many keys in the Florida chain.

What do we call a group of islands like the Florida Keys?

entries.title: Why do the Outer Banks form long, narrow islands?
entries.answer: The Outer Banks are a series of low islands off North Carolina and a small part of Virginia. Waves and currents move sand along the coast. Some of that sand piles up in long strips that nearly follow the mainland shore. A barrier island sits between the open sea and quieter waters and can take much of the push from ocean waves. A storm may open a new gap or move sand, so an island’s shape can change.
facts: Behind many of the islands lie partly sheltered waters called sounds.

entries.title: Why do volcanoes rise along the Cascade Range?
entries.answer: The Cascade Range runs through the Pacific Northwest and into Canada. Some of its tall peaks, such as Mount Rainier and Mount St. Helens, are volcanoes. Off the coast, a smaller piece of Earth’s rocky outer layer is sliding slowly under North America. Deep underground, that movement helps some rock melt. Some melted rock rises and can feed a volcano. Over time, separate volcanoes have grown along more than one part of the mountain range.
facts: Mount St. Helens changed shape during a large eruption in 1980.

How do pieces of Earth’s outer layer move?

entries.title: Why do walkers turn a map to match the ground?
entries.answer: Imagine that a straight road on a map points right, but when you look up, that same stretch of road points straight ahead. You can turn the map so the lines point in the same direction. Now a park on the left side of the road on the map will be on your left as you walk that way. The north arrow or a compass can help when you know which way north is.
facts: Check the north mark because north does not have to be at the top of a map.

questions.text: How does a magnetic compass point?
What do the marks on a map mean?

entries.title: Why does the Colorado Plateau have so many canyons?
entries.answer: The Colorado Plateau is a broad area of high land shared by parts of Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico. Many of its rocks have layers that are still easy to see. The land rose, and rivers cut downward into it over a long time. In some places, the rivers made canyons deep enough to show many layers at once. Elsewhere, erosion left smaller shapes behind, including cliffs, towers and natural arches.
facts: The Grand Canyon is one of the best-known canyons in this high region.

entries.title: Why does water in the Great Basin stay inland?
entries.answer: In the Great Basin, mountain ridges and higher ground surround many valleys. Water that reaches a valley may flow into a small lake or dry lake bed. It may then disappear into the ground or into the air as water vapor. It does not reach the sea in a river. Each drainage basin is the land that sends water to one of these lower places. This region covers much of Nevada and parts of surrounding states. This water rule helps show where the Great Basin is, even if there is no painted line on the ground.
facts: The Great Salt Lake in Utah collects water from rivers and has no river outlet to the sea.

questions.text: What does a map of Nevada’s mountains and valleys look like?

entries.title: Why don’t the Nebraska Sandhills look like a bare desert?
entries.answer: Many hills in central and western Nebraska are made of sand that wind piled up. From a distance, much of this country looks green or brown instead of pale and bare. Grasses cover many of the dunes. Their roots help hold sand, and their stems slow wind close to the ground. Some low areas between the hills hold lakes and marshes. The sand and living plants together give the Sandhills their rolling shape and soft-looking cover.
facts: Many dunes here hold grassland on their slopes, although some patches of sand still show.

entries.title: Why is so much of the Atlantic Coastal Plain low?
entries.answer: In much of the eastern United States, there is a wide strip of low land before the Atlantic Ocean. It is called the Atlantic Coastal Plain. Sand, mud and other loose material built up as rivers, ocean water and wind moved them. Today some parts have flat fields. Other parts have marshes, slow rivers and sandy shores. The ground often gets higher and hillier as you move inland toward the Piedmont. The change can be slow enough to miss on a short walk.
facts: A coastal plain and its underwater edge can both contain many layers of sand and mud.

entries.title: Why is there so much tall grass left in the Flint Hills?
entries.answer: The Flint Hills of Kansas have thin soil and many hard bits of rock near the surface. Their slopes are difficult to plow. As people turned much other prairie into fields, large stretches of this rocky land were used for animals to graze instead. That helped leave room for prairie plants that already grew there. Some grasses get very tall by late summer. Periodic fire also helps keep young trees from taking over many areas.
facts: A hard rock called chert, sometimes called flint, helped give the Flint Hills their name.

entries.title: Why is Washington, D.C., different from a state?
entries.answer: Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States and a place where people live and work. It is a federal district, an area set apart for the country’s government. The letters D.C. stand for District of Columbia. The city sits along the Potomac River, next to Maryland and across water from Virginia. This is far from Washington State, which is in the Pacific Northwest. The two places share a name but have very different locations on a map.
facts: The United States has 50 states, and Washington, D.C., counts as a district rather than one of the 50.

entries.title: Wisconsin
entries.answer: Wisconsin reaches two Great Lakes, Michigan on the east and Superior on the north. Madison, the capital, is farther inland and sits between lakes. The Mississippi River forms part of the western border. In the southwest, a region with steep hills and valleys escaped the ice that covered much of the surrounding land during recent ice ages. That makes the landscape there look very different from many flatter areas to the east.
facts: Madison is between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona.

questions.text: Which five lakes are in the Great Lakes group?

entries.title: Wyoming
entries.answer: Wyoming has Rocky Mountain ranges, broad open basins and plains that continue eastward. Cheyenne, the capital, sits near the southeastern corner where much of that open country begins. In the northwest, some of the land belongs to Yellowstone National Park. There heat underground helps create hot springs and geysers. The snow and water that fall in Wyoming can flow into very different rivers depending on which side of the mountains they land on.
facts: Yellowstone extends into Montana and Idaho, though much of the park is in Wyoming.
